claim: Retrieval practice strengthens new A-C memories compared to restudy.
source: Using a three-day A-B/A-C memory updating paradigm, we found that compared to restudy, retrieval practice could strengthen new A-C memories and reduce old A-B memory intrusion, but did not suppress A-B memories.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from the final memory test showing greater target recall under retrieval practice condition.

claim: Retrieval practice reduces old A-B memory intrusion compared to restudy.
source: Using a three-day A-B/A-C memory updating paradigm, we found that compared to restudy, retrieval practice could strengthen new A-C memories and reduce old A-B memory intrusion, but did not suppress A-B memories.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing fewer competitor intrusions during final test under retrieval practice condition.

claim: Retrieval practice does not suppress A-B memories.
source: Using a three-day A-B/A-C memory updating paradigm, we found that compared to restudy, retrieval practice could strengthen new A-C memories and reduce old A-B memory intrusion, but did not suppress A-B memories.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from Experiments 2 and 3 showing no effect of updating method on A-B memory performance.

claim: Retrieval practice leads to stronger target representation in the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) during the final test compared to restudy.
source: Neural activation pattern analysis revealed that compared to restudy, retrieval practice led to stronger target representation in the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) during the final test.
evidence: Supported by MVPA analysis showing greater target evidence in MPFC for retrieval practice condition.

claim: Under the retrieval practice condition, the MPFC shows strong and comparable competitor evidence for both correct and incorrect trials during final test.
source: Critically, it was only under the retrieval practice condition that the MPFC showed strong and comparable competitor evidence for both correct and incorrect trials during final test, and that the MPFC target representation during updating was predictive of subsequent memory.
evidence: Supported by MVPA analysis showing no significant difference in competitor evidence between correct and incorrect trials under retrieval practice condition in MPFC.

claim: MPFC target representation during updating is predictive of subsequent memory under the retrieval practice condition.
source: Critically, it was only under the retrieval practice condition that the MPFC showed strong and comparable competitor evidence for both correct and incorrect trials during final test, and that the MPFC target representation during updating was predictive of subsequent memory.
evidence: Supported by subsequent memory analysis showing correlation between MPFC target representation during updating and final test performance.

claim: Retrieval practice facilitates memory updating by engaging MPFC mechanisms in memory integration, differentiation and consolidation.
source: These results suggest that retrieval practice is able to facilitate memory updating by strongly engaging MPFC mechanisms in memory integration, differentiation and consolidation.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of MPFC activation and representation during updating and final test.

claim: Successful memory updating involves strengthening the more current memory trace, weakening the older information, and/or differentiating old and new memories.
source: Successful updating of memory involves strengthening the more current memory trace, weakening the older information, and/or differentiating old and new memories, in order to ensure that the old memory is less interfering.
evidence: Based on established understanding of memory updating mechanisms.

claim: Retrieval of learnt information leads to better retention of relevant memory when no obvious interference is involved compared to restudy.
source: Compared to simple restudy of the same material again, retrieval of learnt information leads not only to better retention of relevant memory when no obvious interference is involved (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Pyc and Rawson, 2010), but also to better inhibition of competing, outdated memories (Anderson et al., 1994), reduced proactive interference (Szpunar et al., 2008), enhanced memory integration (Hupbach et al., 2007), and greater susceptibility to subsequent modification (Chan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous behavioral studies.

claim: Retrieval practice leads to better inhibition of competing, outdated memories compared to restudy.
source: Compared to simple restudy of the same material again, retrieval of learnt information leads not only to better retention of relevant memory when no obvious interference is involved (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Pyc and Rawson, 2010), but also to better inhibition of competing, outdated memories (Anderson et al., 1994), reduced proactive interference (Szpunar et al., 2008), enhanced memory integration (Hupbach et al., 2007), and greater susceptibility to subsequent modification (Chan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Anderson et al., 1994.

claim: Retrieval practice leads to reduced proactive interference compared to restudy.
source: Compared to simple restudy of the same material again, retrieval of learnt information leads not only to better retention of relevant memory when no obvious interference is involved (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Pyc and Rawson, 2010), but also to better inhibition of competing, outdated memories (Anderson et al., 1994), reduced proactive interference (Szpunar et al., 2008), enhanced memory integration (Hupbach et al., 2007), and greater susceptibility to subsequent modification (Chan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Szpunar et al., 2008.

claim: Retrieval practice leads to enhanced memory integration compared to restudy.
source: Compared to simple restudy of the same material again, retrieval of learnt information leads not only to better retention of relevant memory when no obvious interference is involved (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Pyc and Rawson, 2010), but also to better inhibition of competing, outdated memories (Anderson et al., 1994), reduced proactive interference (Szpunar et al., 2008), enhanced memory integration (Hupbach et al., 2007), and greater susceptibility to subsequent modification (Chan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hupbach et al., 2007.

claim: Retrieval practice leads to greater susceptibility to subsequent modification compared to restudy.
source: Compared to simple restudy of the same material again, retrieval of learnt information leads not only to better retention of relevant memory when no obvious interference is involved (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008; Pyc and Rawson, 2010), but also to better inhibition of competing, outdated memories (Anderson et al., 1994), reduced proactive interference (Szpunar et al., 2008), enhanced memory integration (Hupbach et al., 2007), and greater susceptibility to subsequent modification (Chan et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chan et al., 2009.

claim: Consolidated memories, when retrieved and reactivated, enter into a transient, labile state, rendering them vulnerable to modification.
source: A large body of work on memory reconsolidation (Dudai, 2006) suggests that consolidated memories, when retrieved and reactivated, enter into a transient, labile state, rendering them vulnerable to modification (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to memory reconsolidation literature.

claim: Electrical shock and pharmacological treatments that block protein synthesis can cause long-lasting impairment of existing memories when they are reactivated.
source: Electrical shock (Kroes et al., 2014) and pharmacological treatments (Kindt et al., 2009; Nader et al., 2000) that block protein synthesis can cause long-lasting impairment of existing memories when they are reactivated.
evidence: Supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Reactivated memories can be disrupted by behavioral methods including retrieval-extinction, counterconditioning, and interference approaches.
source: Reactivated memories can also be disrupted by behavioral methods, including retrieval-extinction (Schiller et al., 2010; Xue et al., 2012), counterconditioning (Goltseker et al., 2017), and interference approaches (James et al., 2015), which have been found to reduce the expression of fear or drug memories and amygdala responses associated with fear (Agren et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral intervention studies.

claim: Reactivated memories can be selectively strengthened, weakened, integrated, and/or differentiated, depending on the mnemonic goals and the characteristics of the reactivated memory.
source: Using representational similarity analysis, recent studies further show that the reactivated memories could be selectively strengthened (Jonker et al., 2018; Lu et al., 2015; Xue et al., 2010), weakened (Wimber et al., 2015), integrated (Schlichting et al., 2015), and/or differentiated (Hulbert and Norman, 2015), depending on the mnemonic goals and the characteristics of the reactivated memory (Tambini and Davachi, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to representational similarity analysis studies.

claim: The medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) plays an important role in the rapid formation of cortical memories, especially during retrieval practice.
source: Emerging studies suggest that the medial prefrontal cortex (MPFC) probably plays an important role in the rapid formation of cortical memories, especially during retrieval practice.
evidence: Based on emerging literature on MPFC function.

claim: Retrieval practice will reactivate related memory traces, and the MPFC is able to develop integrated neocortical representations of these memory traces rapidly.
source: Specifically, it has been hypothesized that retrieval practice will reactivate related memory traces, and that the MPFC is able to develop integrated neocortical representations of these memory traces rapidly, in a way that resembles the characteristics of rapid system consolidation (Antony et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on hypothesis from Antony et al., 2017.

claim: The MPFC is involved in the integration and updating of reactivated memory traces.
source: Consistently, the MPFC has been found to be involved in the integration and updating of reactivated memory traces (Gilboa and Marlatte, 2017; Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to MPFC function studies.

claim: The MPFC is critically involved in encoding novel but related information into existing knowledge.
source: For example, the MPFC is critically involved in encoding novel but related information into existing knowledge (Sommer, 2016), in representing overlapping memories (Tompary and Davachi, 2017), and in inferring relationships between distinct events that share common features (Zeithamova et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sommer, 2016.

claim: The MPFC is involved in representing overlapping memories.
source: For example, the MPFC is critically involved in encoding novel but related information into existing knowledge (Sommer, 2016), in representing overlapping memories (Tompary and Davachi, 2017), and in inferring relationships between distinct events that share common features (Zeithamova et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tompary and Davachi, 2017.

claim: The MPFC is involved in inferring relationships between distinct events that share common features.
source: For example, the MPFC is critically involved in encoding novel but related information into existing knowledge (Sommer, 2016), in representing overlapping memories (Tompary and Davachi, 2017), and in inferring relationships between distinct events that share common features (Zeithamova et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zeithamova et al., 2012.

claim: The lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) may play a role in regulating reactivated memories to support memory changes.
source: Several studies suggest that the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) may play a role in regulating reactivated memories to support memory changes.
evidence: Based on review of LPFC function studies.

claim: The LPFC can bias the competition and reduce the intrusion of unwanted memory in later memory retrieval.
source: First, the LPFC could bias the competition and reduce the intrusion of unwanted memory in later memory retrieval (Kuhl et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kuhl et al., 2012.

claim: Intentional suppression of memory retrieval reduces hippocampal activity via control mechanisms mediated by the LPFC.
source: Intentional suppression of memory retrieval reduces hippocampal activity via control mechanisms mediated by the LPFC (Hulbert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hulbert et al., 2016.

claim: Retrieval practice can suppress or differentiate the neural representation of competitive memories in the sensory cortices or hippocampus, mediated by the LPFC.
source: Second, studies examining retrieval-induced forgetting (Anderson et al., 1994; Norman et al., 2007) have found that retrieval practice could suppress (Wimber et al., 2015) or differentiate (Hulbert and Norman, 2015) the neural representation of competitive memories in the sensory cortices or hippocampus, and that these processes are mediated by the LPFC.
evidence: Supported by citations to retrieval-induced forgetting studies.

claim: Reactivation during wakefulness can destabilize memories and is associated with LPFC activation.
source: Third, reactivation during wakefulness has been found to destabilize memories and has been associated with LPFC activation (Diekelmann et al., 2011), supporting its role in modifying reactivated memory representations.
evidence: Supported by citation to Diekelmann et al., 2011.

claim: During updating, retrieval practice elicits greater reactivation of the outdated competitor (B) than restudy exposures.
source: We hypothesized that during updating, retrieval practice would elicit greater reactivation of the outdated competitor (i.e., B) than would restudy exposures, reflecting the greater tendency of retrieval to trigger competition that requires correction.
evidence: This is a hypothesis that was tested and confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: During the final memory test, retrieval practice leads to stronger reactivation of the replacement memory (C) compared to restudy.
source: Despite these added difficulties, we predicted that during the final memory test, retrieval practice would lead to a better long-term effect: stronger reactivation of the replacement memory (i.e., the target, C) as well as weaker reactivation of the outdated competitor.
evidence: This is a prediction that was confirmed by the experimental data.

claim: During the final memory test, retrieval practice leads to weaker reactivation of the outdated competitor (B) compared to restudy.
source: Despite these added difficulties, we predicted that during the final memory test, retrieval practice would lead to a better long-term effect: stronger reactivation of the replacement memory (i.e., the target, C) as well as weaker reactivation of the outdated competitor.
evidence: This is a prediction that was tested in the study.

claim: Subjects recalled more updated targets during the final memory test for pairs updated under the RetPrac condition compared to the Restudy condition (t(18) = 5.37, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.30).
source: During the final memory test administered on Day 3, subjects recalled more updated targets (t(18) = 5.37, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.30, Figure 1B) with shorter response time (t(18) = −4.13, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.35), and showed fewer memory intrusions (i.e., accidental recall of the outdated competitors) (t(18) = −4.47, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.04) for pairs updated under the RetPrac condition compared to those updated under the Restudy condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Subjects had shorter response times during the final memory test for pairs updated under the RetPrac condition compared to the Restudy condition (t(18) = −4.13, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.35).
source: During the final memory test administered on Day 3, subjects recalled more updated targets (t(18) = 5.37, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.30, Figure 1B) with shorter response time (t(18) = −4.13, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.35), and showed fewer memory intrusions (i.e., accidental recall of the outdated competitors) (t(18) = −4.47, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.04) for pairs updated under the RetPrac condition compared to those updated under the Restudy condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data.

claim: Subjects showed fewer memory intrusions during the final memory test for pairs updated under the RetPrac condition compared to the Restudy condition (t(18) = −4.47, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.04).
source: During the final memory test administered on Day 3, subjects recalled more updated targets (t(18) = 5.37, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.30, Figure 1B) with shorter response time (t(18) = −4.13, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.35), and showed fewer memory intrusions (i.e., accidental recall of the outdated competitors) (t(18) = −4.47, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.04) for pairs updated under the RetPrac condition compared to those updated under the Restudy condition.
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During acquisition of the replacement memory on Day 2, retrieval practice performance improved dramatically across the three practice repetitions, as indicated by increased ability to recall the target response category (F(2, 36)=137.11, p<0.001).
source: During the acquisition of the replacement memory on Day 2, updating, retrieval practice performance was initially near the chance level, but it improved dramatically across the three practice repetitions, as indicated by increased ability to recall the target response category (F(2, 36)=137.11, p<0.001), and by decreased production of responses in the competitor category (F(2, 36)=9.82, p<0.001) or 'other' responses (F(2, 36)=42.69, p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during updating and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During acquisition of the replacement memory on Day 2, retrieval practice showed decreased production of responses in the competitor category across repetitions (F(2, 36)=9.82, p<0.001).
source: During the acquisition of the replacement memory on Day 2, updating, retrieval practice performance was initially near the chance level, but it improved dramatically across the three practice repetitions, as indicated by increased ability to recall the target response category (F(2, 36)=137.11, p<0.001), and by decreased production of responses in the competitor category (F(2, 36)=9.82, p<0.001) or 'other' responses (F(2, 36)=42.69, p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during updating and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: During acquisition of the replacement memory on Day 2, retrieval practice showed decreased production of 'other' responses across repetitions (F(2, 36)=42.69, p<0.001).
source: During the acquisition of the replacement memory on Day 2, updating, retrieval practice performance was initially near the chance level, but it improved dramatically across the three practice repetitions, as indicated by increased ability to recall the target response category (F(2, 36)=137.11, p<0.001), and by decreased production of responses in the competitor category (F(2, 36)=9.82, p<0.001) or 'other' responses (F(2, 36)=42.69, p<0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during updating and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Behavioral performance for the restudy trials was near perfect across the three repetitions (accuracy = 99.0%, and no difference across repetitions F(2, 36)=0.42, p=0.66).
source: By contrast, behavioral performance for the restudy trials was near perfect across the three repetitions, reflecting the ease in processing material that is simply presented for re-study when no retrieval demand is involved (accuracy = 99.0%, and no difference across repetitions F(2, 36)=0.42, p=0.66).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data during updating.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects showed greater A-C memory under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition during the A-C memory test, as indicated by significantly higher correct recall of targets (t(45) = 3.93, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.57).
source: Replicating the main effect, we found greater A-C memory under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition during the A-C memory test, as indicated by the significantly higher correct recall of targets (t(45) = 3.93, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.57) and fewer competitor intrusions (t(45) = −2.75, p=0.008, Cohen's d = 0.36) under the RetPrac than under the Restudy condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects showed fewer competitor intrusions under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition during the A-C memory test (t(45) = −2.75, p=0.008, Cohen's d = 0.36).
source: Replicating the main effect, we found greater A-C memory under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition during the A-C memory test, as indicated by the significantly higher correct recall of targets (t(45) = 3.93, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.57) and fewer competitor intrusions (t(45) = −2.75, p=0.008, Cohen's d = 0.36) under the RetPrac than under the Restudy condition (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Experiment 2, A-B memory was very strong during A-B recall (55.9% correct) and showed no effect of updating method on either B memory (t(45) = 1.43, p=0.19) or C intrusion (t(45) = 0.80, p=0.43).
source: However, we found that A-B memory was very strong during A-B recall (55.9% correct) and showed no effect of updating method on either B memory (t(45) = 1.43, p=0.19) or C intrusion (t(45) = 0.80, p=0.43).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, correct trials in the A-C memory test showed more C memory intrusions during the A-B test than did the incorrect trials (t(45) = 3.38, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.71).
source: Consistently, we found that the correct trials in the A-C memory test (reflecting strong A-C memory) showed more C memory intrusions overall during the A-B test than did the incorrect trials (t(45) = 3.38, p=0.001, Cohen's d = 0.71).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2.

claim: In Experiment 2, the C memory intrusion rate during A-B test was numerically smaller in the RetPrac condition than in the Restudy condition (t(45) = −1.59, p=0.12).
source: Interestingly, the intrusion rate was numerically smaller in the RetPrac condition than in the Restudy condition (t(45) = −1.59, p=0.12), which is consistent with the differentiation hypothesis (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2B.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects made more correct responses in both A-B and A-C tests under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition (24.0% vs 19.7%, t(45) = 3.81, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.48).
source: We found that subjects made more correct responses in both tests under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition (24.0% vs 19.7%, t(45) = 3.81, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.48), but showed less B memory (21.0% vs 23.2%, t(45) = −2.61, p=0.012, Cohen's d = 0.25), and comparable C memory (11.7% vs 11.5%, t(45) = 0.18, p=0.86) in both memory tests (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by joint analysis of A-B and A-C memory test data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects showed less B memory in both A-B and A-C tests under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition (21.0% vs 23.2%, t(45) = −2.61, p=0.012, Cohen's d = 0.25).
source: We found that subjects made more correct responses in both tests under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition (24.0% vs 19.7%, t(45) = 3.81, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.48), but showed less B memory (21.0% vs 23.2%, t(45) = −2.61, p=0.012, Cohen's d = 0.25), and comparable C memory (11.7% vs 11.5%, t(45) = 0.18, p=0.86) in both memory tests (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by joint analysis of A-B and A-C memory test data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Experiment 2, subjects showed comparable C memory in both A-B and A-C tests between RetPrac and Restudy conditions (11.7% vs 11.5%, t(45) = 0.18, p=0.86).
source: We found that subjects made more correct responses in both tests under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition (24.0% vs 19.7%, t(45) = 3.81, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.48), but showed less B memory (21.0% vs 23.2%, t(45) = −2.61, p=0.012, Cohen's d = 0.25), and comparable C memory (11.7% vs 11.5%, t(45) = 0.18, p=0.86) in both memory tests (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by joint analysis of A-B and A-C memory test data from Experiment 2 and shown in Figure 2C.

claim: In Experiment 3, subjects showed significantly higher correct item recall under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition during A-C memory test (t(27) = 8.06, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.50).
source: Our findings again replicated the retrieval-practice effect on A-C memory, as indicated by the significantly higher correct item recall (t(27) = 8.06, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.50) under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition, but comparable performance on the A-B memory test (t(27) = 0.81, p=0.43) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: In Experiment 3, subjects showed comparable performance on the A-B memory test between RetPrac and Restudy conditions (t(27) = 0.81, p=0.43).
source: Our findings again replicated the retrieval-practice effect on A-C memory, as indicated by the significantly higher correct item recall (t(27) = 8.06, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.50) under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition, but comparable performance on the A-B memory test (t(27) = 0.81, p=0.43) (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of behavioral data from Experiment 3 and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the MPFC (39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001).
source: Confirming the relevance of these regions to our task, we found that the classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the MPFC, VTC, and AG (ranging from 39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001, all survived FDR correction), but not in the HPC (35.5%, p=0.35) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the VTC (39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001).
source: Confirming the relevance of these regions to our task, we found that the classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the MPFC, VTC, and AG (ranging from 39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001, all survived FDR correction), but not in the HPC (35.5%, p=0.35) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the AG (39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001).
source: Confirming the relevance of these regions to our task, we found that the classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the MPFC, VTC, and AG (ranging from 39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001, all survived FDR correction), but not in the HPC (35.5%, p=0.35) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The classifier output could not predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test above chance in the HPC (35.5%, p=0.35).
source: Confirming the relevance of these regions to our task, we found that the classifier output could predict subjects' categorical judgments during the final test with significantly above-chance accuracy in the MPFC, VTC, and AG (ranging from 39.6% to 42.6%, all p-values <0.001, all survived FDR correction), but not in the HPC (35.5%, p=0.35) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In the MPFC, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant evidence-by-outcome interaction (F(1,18) = 23.25, p=0.0001).
source: In the MPFC, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant evidence-by-outcome interaction (F(1,18) = 23.25, p=0.0001, survived FDR correction, Figure 3B), suggesting that the activation in the MPFC tracked behavioral performance.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of MPFC data and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the MPFC, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant method-by-evidence interaction (F(1,18) = 6.50, p=0.02).
source: We also found a significant method-by-evidence interaction (F(1,18) = 6.50, p=0.02, survived FDR correction).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of MPFC data.

claim: In the MPFC, for target reactivation, there were significant main effects of updating method (F(1,18) = 7.01, p=0.02) and outcome (F(1,18) = 15.10, p=0.001).
source: For target reactivation, there were significant main effects of updating method (RetPrac vs Restudy) (F(1,18) = 7.01, p=0.02, Supplementary file 2b) and outcome (chosen targets vs chosen competitors) (F(1,18) = 15.10, p=0.001, survived FDR correction), suggesting that correct responses were associated with stronger target evidence reactivation, and that retrieval practice was able to boost the target reactivation for both correct and incorrect trials.
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA analysis of MPFC target reactivation data.

claim: In the MPFC, for competitor evidence, there was stronger competitor evidence reactivation for incorrect trials than for correct trials under the Restudy condition (t(18) = 3.46, p=0.003, Cohen's d = 0.86).
source: For competitor evidence, however, we found that there was stronger competitor evidence reactivation for incorrect trials than for correct trials under the Restudy condition (t(18) = 3.46, p=0.003, Cohen's d = 0.86, survived FDR correction), whereas no such difference was found for the RetPrac condition (t(18) = 0.35, p=0.73), although the outcome-by-condition interaction did not reach significance (F(1,18) = 2.53, p=0.13, Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MPFC competitor evidence data.

claim: In the MPFC, for competitor evidence, no difference was found between correct and incorrect trials under the RetPrac condition (t(18) = 0.35, p=0.73).
source: For competitor evidence, however, we found that there was stronger competitor evidence reactivation for incorrect trials than for correct trials under the Restudy condition (t(18) = 3.46, p=0.003, Cohen's d = 0.86, survived FDR correction), whereas no such difference was found for the RetPrac condition (t(18) = 0.35, p=0.73), although the outcome-by-condition interaction did not reach significance (F(1,18) = 2.53, p=0.13, Supplementary file 2b).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of MPFC competitor evidence data.

claim: In the AG, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant evidence-by-outcome interaction (F(1,18) = 18.46, p=0.0004).
source: In the AG, three-way ANOVA also revealed significant a evidence-by-outcome interaction (F(1,18) = 18.46, p=0.0004, survived FDR correction, Figure 3B), suggesting that the representation in the AG tracked behavioral performance.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of AG data and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the AG, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant method-by-evidence interaction (F(1,18) = 7.45, p=0.01).
source: We also found a significant method-by-evidence interaction (F(1,18) = 7.45, p=0.01, survived FDR correction).
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of AG data.

claim: In the AG, for target reactivation, there was a significant main effect of response type (F(1,18) = 7.23, p=0.02), with stronger target evidence for correct responses than for incorrect responses.
source: For target reactivation, there was a significant main effect of response type (F(1,18) = 7.23, p=0.02, survived FDR correction, Supplementary file 2b), with stronger target evidence for correct responses than for incorrect responses.
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA analysis of AG target reactivation data.

claim: In the AG, for competitor reactivation, there was a significant main effect of response type (F(1,18) = 6.04, p=0.02), with stronger competitor evidence for incorrect responses than for correct responses.
source: For competitor reactivation, there was a significant main effect of response type (F(1,18) = 6.04, p=0.02, Supplementary file 2b), with stronger competitor evidence for incorrect responses than for correct responses.
evidence: Supported by two-way ANOVA analysis of AG competitor reactivation data.

claim: In the VTC, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant evidence-by-outcome interaction (F(1,18) = 26.51, p<0.0001).
source: In the VTC, we also found a significant evidence-by-outcome interaction (F(1,18) = 26.51, p<0.0001, survived FDR correction, Figure 3B), again suggesting that the representation in the VTC tracked behavioral performance.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of VTC data and shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In the VTC, three-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of method (F(1,18) = 5.58, p=0.03).
source: Interestingly, we found a significant main effect of method (F(1,18) = 5.58, p=0.03), which did not interact with other factors (p-values >0.20, Supplementary file 2a), suggesting that retrieval practice significantly suppressed competitor evidence (F(1,18) = 4.68, p=0.04) and marginally reduced the target evidence (F(1,18) = 3.26, p=0.09) in the VTC.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of VTC data.

claim: In the VTC, retrieval practice significantly suppressed competitor evidence (F(1,18) = 4.68, p=0.04).
source: Interestingly, we found a significant main effect of method (F(1,18) = 5.58, p=0.03), which did not interact with other factors (p-values >0.20, Supplementary file 2a), suggesting that retrieval practice significantly suppressed competitor evidence (F(1,18) = 4.68, p=0.04) and marginally reduced the target evidence (F(1,18) = 3.26, p=0.09) in the VTC.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of VTC data.

claim: In the VTC, retrieval practice marginally reduced the target evidence (F(1,18) = 3.26, p=0.09).
source: Interestingly, we found a significant main effect of method (F(1,18) = 5.58, p=0.03), which did not interact with other factors (p-values >0.20, Supplementary file 2a), suggesting that retrieval practice significantly suppressed competitor evidence (F(1,18) = 4.68, p=0.04) and marginally reduced the target evidence (F(1,18) = 3.26, p=0.09) in the VTC.
evidence: Supported by ANOVA analysis of VTC data.

claim: During restudy, correctly recalled items showed stronger target activation than did incorrectly recalled ones in the VTC (t(18) = 4.29, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.79).
source: This analysis revealed distinct patterns for the Restudy and RetPrac conditions: correctly recalled items (i.e., target) showed stronger target activation than did incorrectly recalled ones (i.e., competitor) in the VTC (t(18) = 4.29, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.79, survived FDR correction) during restudy (all other ROIs, p-values >0.13), whereas retrieval practiced items that were later correctly recalled were associated with stronger target activation than incorrectly recalled ones in the MPFC (t(18) = 2.66, p=0.016, Cohen's d = 0.60, survived FDR correction, Figure 4A) (all other ROIs, p-values >0.12).
evidence: Supported by subsequent memory analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: During retrieval practice, items that were later correctly recalled were associated with stronger target activation than incorrectly recalled ones in the MPFC (t(18) = 2.66, p=0.016, Cohen's d = 0.60).
source: This analysis revealed distinct patterns for the Restudy and RetPrac conditions: correctly recalled items (i.e., target) showed stronger target activation than did incorrectly recalled ones (i.e., competitor) in the VTC (t(18) = 4.29, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 0.79, survived FDR correction) during restudy (all other ROIs, p-values >0.13), whereas retrieval practiced items that were later correctly recalled were associated with stronger target activation than incorrectly recalled ones in the MPFC (t(18) = 2.66, p=0.016, Cohen's d = 0.60, survived FDR correction, Figure 4A) (all other ROIs, p-values >0.12).
evidence: Supported by subsequent memory analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Under the RetPrac condition, there was significant competitor reactivation (compared with 'other' evidence) in the MPFC (t(18) = 3.26, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.98).
source: As predicted, we found significant competitor reactivation (compared with 'other' evidence) under the RetPrac condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 3.26, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.98), VTC (t(18) = 3.20, p=0.005, Cohen's d = 1.03), and AG (t(18) = 4.31, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.34), all survived FDR correction (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis during updating and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under the RetPrac condition, there was significant competitor reactivation (compared with 'other' evidence) in the VTC (t(18) = 3.20, p=0.005, Cohen's d = 1.03).
source: As predicted, we found significant competitor reactivation (compared with 'other' evidence) under the RetPrac condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 3.26, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.98), VTC (t(18) = 3.20, p=0.005, Cohen's d = 1.03), and AG (t(18) = 4.31, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.34), all survived FDR correction (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis during updating and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under the RetPrac condition, there was significant competitor reactivation (compared with 'other' evidence) in the AG (t(18) = 4.31, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.34).
source: As predicted, we found significant competitor reactivation (compared with 'other' evidence) under the RetPrac condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 3.26, p=0.004, Cohen's d = 0.98), VTC (t(18) = 3.20, p=0.005, Cohen's d = 1.03), and AG (t(18) = 4.31, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.34), all survived FDR correction (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis during updating and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Under the Restudy condition, there was no evidence of reactivation of the outdated competitors in any of the three ROIs (all p-values >0.13).
source: By contrast, there was no evidence of reactivation of the outdated competitors in any of the three ROIs in the Restudy condition (all p-values >0.13).
evidence: Supported by classifier analysis during updating.

claim: There was significantly stronger competitor reactivation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 4.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.36).
source: Direct comparisons revealed significantly stronger competitor reactivation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 4.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.36), VTC (t(18) = 10.87, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 3.46), and AG (t(18) = 6.98, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.21), again all survived FDR correction.
evidence: Supported by direct comparison of classifier outputs during updating.

claim: There was significantly stronger competitor reactivation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition in the VTC (t(18) = 10.87, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 3.46).
source: Direct comparisons revealed significantly stronger competitor reactivation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 4.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.36), VTC (t(18) = 10.87, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 3.46), and AG (t(18) = 6.98, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.21), again all survived FDR correction.
evidence: Supported by direct comparison of classifier outputs during updating.

claim: There was significantly stronger competitor reactivation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition in the AG (t(18) = 6.98, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.21).
source: Direct comparisons revealed significantly stronger competitor reactivation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition in the MPFC (t(18) = 4.32, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 1.36), VTC (t(18) = 10.87, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 3.46), and AG (t(18) = 6.98, p<0.001, Cohen's d = 2.21), again all survived FDR correction.
evidence: Supported by direct comparison of classifier outputs during updating.

claim: Across the three repetitions, target evidence increased with the number of repetitions in the VTC (t(18) = 3.44, p=0.003).
source: Across the three repetitions, we found that the target evidence increased with the number of repetitions in the VTC (t(18) = 3.44, p=0.003), but not in the MPFC (t(18) = 1.75, p=0.10) or AG (t(18) = 1.78, p=0.09) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of target evidence across repetitions and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Across the three repetitions, target evidence did not increase with the number of repetitions in the MPFC (t(18) = 1.75, p=0.10).
source: Across the three repetitions, we found that the target evidence increased with the number of repetitions in the VTC (t(18) = 3.44, p=0.003), but not in the MPFC (t(18) = 1.75, p=0.10) or AG (t(18) = 1.78, p=0.09) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of target evidence across repetitions and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Across the three repetitions, target evidence did not increase with the number of repetitions in the AG (t(18) = 1.78, p=0.09).
source: Across the three repetitions, we found that the target evidence increased with the number of repetitions in the VTC (t(18) = 3.44, p=0.003), but not in the MPFC (t(18) = 1.75, p=0.10) or AG (t(18) = 1.78, p=0.09) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by analysis of target evidence across repetitions and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: There was no significant reduction in competitor evidence across repetitions (all p-values >0.73).
source: Strikingly, although subjects made fewer competitor responses across repetitions, we did not find a significant reduction in competitor evidence across repetitions (all p-values >0.73).
evidence: Supported by analysis of competitor evidence across repetitions.

claim: VTC showed a pattern highly consistent with the nonmonotonic plasticity model under the RetPrac condition [P(Theory consistent)=0.836, p=0.012].
source: The results suggest that VTC showed a pattern that was highly consistent with the model under the RetPrac condition [P(Theory consistent)=0.836, p=0.012, Figure 4C].
evidence: Supported by Bayesian curve-fitting analysis and shown in Figure 4C.

claim: MPFC did not show a pattern consistent with the nonmonotonic plasticity model under the RetPrac condition [P(Theory consistent)=0.526].
source: No such pattern was found in the MPFC [P(Theory consistent)=0.526] and the model fitting failed for the AG.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian curve-fitting analysis.

claim: Model fitting for the nonmonotonic plasticity hypothesis failed for the AG under the RetPrac condition.
source: No such pattern was found in the MPFC [P(Theory consistent)=0.526] and the model fitting failed for the AG.
evidence: Supported by Bayesian curve-fitting analysis.

claim: All model fitting in MPFC, VTC, and AG failed under the Restudy condition.
source: All model fitting in these three regions failed under the Restudy condition (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by Bayesian curve-fitting analysis and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Updating by retrieval practice engaged the left lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus (dACC), bilateral anterior insular cortex (AI), and caudate nucleus more than did updating by restudy.
source: We found that updating by retrieval practice engaged the left lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus (dACC), bilateral anterior insular cortex (AI), and caudate nucleus (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3a) more than did updating by restudy, whereas the hippocampus and other regions showed significantly weaker activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: Supported by univariate fMRI analysis comparing RetPrac and Restudy conditions and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The hippocampus and other regions showed significantly weaker activation during retrieval practice compared to restudy.
source: We found that updating by retrieval practice engaged the left lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC), dorsal anterior cingulate gyrus (dACC), bilateral anterior insular cortex (AI), and caudate nucleus (Figure 5A, Supplementary file 3a) more than did updating by restudy, whereas the hippocampus and other regions showed significantly weaker activation (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 3b).
evidence: Supported by univariate fMRI analysis comparing RetPrac and Restudy conditions and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The left LPFC activation for LC trials was significantly lower than that for FC trials (t(18) = −7.17, p<0.001).
source: Consistently, we found that the left LPFC activation for LC trials was significantly lower than that for FC trials (t(18) = −7.17, p<0.001) and IC trials (t(18) = −4.76, p<0.001) (Figure 5B), suggesting that the left LPFC activation was mainly driven by the extent of memory competition.
evidence: Supported by analysis of LPFC activation by trial type and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The left LPFC activation for LC trials was significantly lower than that for IC trials (t(18) = −4.76, p<0.001).
source: Consistently, we found that the left LPFC activation for LC trials was significantly lower than that for FC trials (t(18) = −7.17, p<0.001) and IC trials (t(18) = −4.76, p<0.001) (Figure 5B), suggesting that the left LPFC activation was mainly driven by the extent of memory competition.
evidence: Supported by analysis of LPFC activation by trial type and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The caudate activation for the FC trials was significantly greater than that for the other two types of trials (all p-values <0.004).
source: By contrast, the caudate activation for the FC trials was significantly greater than that for the other two types of trials (all p-values <0.004, Supplementary file 3c), consistent with its role in prediction-error-based processing.
evidence: Supported by analysis of caudate activation by trial type.

claim: Strong caudate activation was associated with greater competitor evidence reduction in the next repetition in the VTC (χ2(1)=5.86, p=0.015).
source: This revealed that strong caudate activation was associated with greater competitor evidence reduction in the next repetition in the VTC (χ2(1)=5.86, p=0.015), but not in MPFC or AG (all p-values >0.15), suggesting that the VTC evidence could be temporary weakened by reinforcement learning.
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects modeling analysis.

claim: Strong caudate activation was not associated with competitor evidence reduction in the next repetition in MPFC or AG (all p-values >0.15).
source: This revealed that strong caudate activation was associated with greater competitor evidence reduction in the next repetition in the VTC (χ2(1)=5.86, p=0.015), but not in MPFC or AG (all p-values >0.15), suggesting that the VTC evidence could be temporary weakened by reinforcement learning.
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects modeling analysis.

claim: Trials with greater LPFC activity during retrieval practice showed superior memory updating (target – competitor evidence) during the final test on Day 3 in the MPFC (χ2(1)=4.62, p=0.032).
source: This analysis revealed that trials with greater LPFC activity during retrieval practice ultimately showed superior memory updating (i.e., target – competitor evidence) during the final test on Day 3 in the MPFC (χ2(1)=4.62, p=0.032), but no effect was found in the caudate.
evidence: Supported by mixed-effects modeling analysis.

claim: Retrieval practice had no effect on A-B memory, albeit it significantly enhanced new memory and reduced old memory intrusions in the A-C memory test.
source: We found that retrieval practice had no effect on A-B memory, albeit it significantly enhanced new memory and reduced old memory intrusions in the A-C memory test.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data from Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: Reduced intrusions could be achieved without significantly suppressing the old memories, but by strengthening the new memory traces and differentiating the old and new memory traces.
source: In any case, our results suggest that reduced intrusions could be achieved without significantly suppressing the old memories, but by strengthening the new memory traces and differentiating the old and new memory traces.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of behavioral results across experiments.

claim: Retrieval practice could shift the neural substrates from VTC to MPFC, which is involved in fast system consolidation.
source: First, we found that retrieval practice could shift the neural substrates from VTC to MPFC, which is involved in fast system consolidation (Antony et al., 2017).
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of subsequent memory effects and supported by citation.

claim: During retrieval, item-specific reactivation is generally not found in the VTC.
source: Existing studies have shown that during retrieval, item-specific reactivation is generally not found in the VTC (Favila et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Retrieval practice does not improve the quality of sensory memory.
source: These features are consistent with the behavioral findings that retrieval practice does not improve the quality of sensory memory (Sutterer and Awh, 2016), and may promote gist-based false memory (McDermott, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Retrieval practice may promote gist-based false memory.
source: These features are consistent with the behavioral findings that retrieval practice does not improve the quality of sensory memory (Sutterer and Awh, 2016), and may promote gist-based false memory (McDermott, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to McDermott, 2006.

claim: Feedback has been consistently shown to improve memory performance.
source: Although existing studies have found a significant effect of retrieval practice when no feedback was provided (Karpicke and Roediger, 2008), feedback has been consistently shown to improve memory performance (Butler and Roediger, 2008; Pashler et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to feedback studies.

claim: The caudate is involved in processing positive prediction error.
source: The current study also found greater caudate activation under the RetPrac condition, in particular for the first correct trial, which is consistent with its role in processing positive prediction error (O'Doherty et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation and consistent with current findings.

claim: Prediction error plays an important role in memory updating and reconsolidation.
source: Recent studies suggest that prediction error plays an important role in memory updating (Kim et al., 2014) and reconsolidation (Lee et al., 2017), and that the caudate is involved in modifying and re-encoding the retrieved memory representation (Scimeca and Badre, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: The caudate is involved in modifying and re-encoding the retrieved memory representation.
source: Recent studies suggest that prediction error plays an important role in memory updating (Kim et al., 2014) and reconsolidation (Lee et al., 2017), and that the caudate is involved in modifying and re-encoding the retrieved memory representation (Scimeca and Badre, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scimeca and Badre, 2012.

claim: Retrieval practice is an effortful process as compared to simple restudy.
source: Third, retrieval practice is an effortful process as compared to simple restudy.
evidence: Based on general understanding of retrieval practice.

claim: Neuroimaging studies have found greater neural activity during retrieval than during restudy.
source: Consistently, neuroimaging studies have found greater neural activity during retrieval than during restudy (Wing et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wing et al., 2013.

claim: Retrieval practice can potentiate subsequent learning, which is associated with greater frontoparietal activity.
source: In addition, retrieval practice could also potentiate subsequent learning, which is associated with greater frontoparietal activity (Nelson et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nelson et al., 2013.

claim: The LPFC is involved in controlled memory retrieval among competitors.
source: We further found that LPFC activation was greater when there was a greater competitor intrusion, which is consistent with its role in controlled memory retrieval among competitors (Badre et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by current findings and citation to Badre et al., 2005.

claim: The LPFC is implicated in reducing the intrusion of competitors in memory retrieval.
source: Previous studies have further implicated the LPFC in reducing the intrusion of competitors in memory retrieval (Kuhl et al., 2012), and in reducing competition memories through cortical pattern suppression (Wimber et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The LPFC is implicated in reducing competition memories through cortical pattern suppression.
source: Previous studies have further implicated the LPFC in reducing the intrusion of competitors in memory retrieval (Kuhl et al., 2012), and in reducing competition memories through cortical pattern suppression (Wimber et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wimber et al., 2015.

claim: The MPFC has been implicated in memory integration and updating.
source: The MPFC has been implicated in memory integration and updating (Preston and Eichenbaum, 2013; Zeithamova et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Memory integration can occur even when competing memories are simultaneously reactivated.
source: Our results replicated and extended these observations by showing that memory integration could occur even when competing memories were simultaneously reactivated.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of MPFC results showing comparable competitor evidence for correct and incorrect trials.

claim: The MPFC is able to develop rapidly integrated neocortical representations of reactivated memory traces during retrieval practice.
source: This fits very well with the hypothesis that MPFC is able to develop rapidly integrated neocortical representations of reactivated memory traces during retrieval practice (Antony et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Antony et al., 2017 and consistent with current findings.

claim: The angular gyrus exhibits abstract yet item-specific mnemonic representations.
source: Consistently, other studies have shown that the angular gyrus exhibits abstract yet item-specific mnemonic representations (Kuhl and Chun, 2014; Xiao et al., 2017), which is modulated by mnemonic goals (Favila et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The representations in the angular gyrus can serve as a mnemonic buffer that helps to make mnemonic decisions.
source: Through its connection with the more anterior region, i.e., the lateral intraparietal sulcus (latIPS), the representations in the angular gyrus can serve as a mnemonic buffer that helps to make mnemonic decisions (Sestieri et al., 2017; Wagner et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The angular gyrus functions as a multimodal convergent zone to combine memory signals from multiple brain regions and to form a memory representation that is closely related to subjective experience and memory decisions.
source: Our results support the idea that AG functions as a multimodal convergent zone to combine memory signals from multiple brain regions and to form a memory representation that is closely related to subjective experience and memory decisions.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of AG results showing close tracking of behavioral performance.

claim: Successful memory retrieval is often associated with greater hippocampal activity.
source: Successful memory retrieval is often associated with greater hippocampal activity.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of hippocampal function.

claim: Weaker hippocampal activation was observed under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition.
source: Interestingly, we observed weaker hippocampal activation under the RetPrac condition than under the Restudy condition.
evidence: Supported by univariate fMRI analysis.

claim: The hippocampus might be inhibited when subjects are required to suppress thoughts and memories.
source: Previous studies suggested that the hippocampus might be inhibited when subjects were required to suppress thoughts and memories (Benoit and Anderson, 2012; Hulbert et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The MPFC represented task-related information that was related to subsequent memory performance.
source: For example, although the MPFC also showed weaker activation under the RetPrac condition, MVPA analysis suggested that the MPFC represented task-related information that was related to subsequent memory performance (Figure 4A), suggesting that it played an important role in memory updating.
evidence: Supported by MVPA analysis and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The sparse nature of hippocampal representation, the low signal-to-noise ratio in this region, and/or the weak categorical representation might account for the lower classifier accuracy in the hippocampus.
source: This might be due to the sparse nature of hippocampal representation (Quiroga et al., 2008), the low signal-to-noise ratio in this region, and/or the weak categorical representation.
evidence: Speculative explanation based on known properties of hippocampal representation and supported by citation.

claim: Memory representation can be transformed from encoding to retrieval.
source: Previous studies have shown that memory representation could be transformed from encoding to retrieval (Chen et al., 2017; Xiao et al., 2017; Xue, 2018), and that this transformation could have further reduced the classifier performance (Albers et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reactivation of a target memory will strengthen the activated memory.
source: On the one hand, reactivation of a target memory will strengthen the activated memory (Tambini and Davachi, 2019; Xue, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Reactivation of unwanted memories (e.g., competitors) can facilitate the suppression of those unwanted memories.
source: On the other hand, reactivation of unwanted memories (e.g., competitors) can facilitate the suppression of those unwanted memories (Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2017.

claim: Reactivation (via retrieval practice) can integrate and differentiate co-activated memories.
source: Beyond the mechanisms of strengthening and weakening memory representations to achieve memory updating, the current study adds to the growing literature reporting that reactivation (via retrieval practice) can also integrate and differentiate co-activated memories (Chan et al., 2009; Hulbert and Norman, 2015; Schlichting et al., 2015; Zeithamova et al., 2012) and hence can increase the flexibility of memory updating in different contexts.
evidence: Supported by current findings and citations to previous studies.

claim: Nineteen healthy college students (seven males; mean age = 21.5 years, range = 18–25 years) participated in the fMRI study.
source: Nineteen healthy college students (seven males; mean age = 21.5 years, range = 18–25 years) participated in the fMRI study, and two additional samples of 46 (18 males; mean age = 22.6 years, range = 18–29 years) and 28 college students (five males; mean age = 21.0 years, range = 18–24 years) participated the two behavior experiments (Exps 2 and 3), respectively.
evidence: Description of study participants.

claim: 46 college students (18 males; mean age = 22.6 years, range = 18–29 years) participated in Experiment 2.
source: Nineteen healthy college students (seven males; mean age = 21.5 years, range = 18–25 years) participated in the fMRI study, and two additional samples of 46 (18 males; mean age = 22.6 years, range = 18–29 years) and 28 college students (five males; mean age = 21.0 years, range = 18–24 years) participated the two behavior experiments (Exps 2 and 3), respectively.
evidence: Description of study participants.

claim: 28 college students (five males; mean age = 21.0 years, range = 18–24 years) participated in Experiment 3.
source: Nineteen healthy college students (seven males; mean age = 21.5 years, range = 18–25 years) participated in the fMRI study, and two additional samples of 46 (18 males; mean age = 22.6 years, range = 18–29 years) and 28 college students (five males; mean age = 21.0 years, range = 18–24 years) participated the two behavior experiments (Exps 2 and 3), respectively.
evidence: Description of study participants.

claim: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards at Beijing Normal University and the Center for MRI Research at Peking University.
source: The study was approved by the Institutional Review Boards at Beijing Normal University and the Center for MRI Research at Peking University.
evidence: Statement of ethical approval.

claim: Stimuli consisted of 144 Chinese words (cues) and 288 pictures (associates).
source: Stimuli consisted of 144 Chinese words (cues) and 288 pictures (associates).
evidence: Description of experimental materials.

claim: Pictures were color photographs from three categories, including famous faces, common objects, and famous scenes.
source: Pictures were color photographs from three categories, including famous faces (e.g., Jet Li), common objects (e.g., toothbrush), and famous scenes (e.g., the Forbidden City).
evidence: Description of experimental materials.

claim: Each word was associated with two pictures from different categories.
source: Each word was associated with two pictures from different categories (e.g., A-B, word-face associations; A-C, word-object associations).
evidence: Description of experimental design.

claim: The whole experiment lasted for three consecutive days.
source: The whole experiment lasted for three consecutive days.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: On Day 1, subjects were trained on the 144 word-picture associations (A-B learning).
source: On Day 1, subjects were trained on the 144 word-picture associations (A-B learning).
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.

claim: On Day 2, subjects were asked to update the old memory with the new A-C associations, half under the RetPrac condition and the other half under the Restudy condition.
source: On Day 2, subjects were asked to update the old memory with the new A-C associations, half under the RetPrac condition and the other half under the Restudy condition.
evidence: Description of experimental procedure.
